titre: Nobody was looking for a fiber
accroche: In 1928, DuPont funds research with no commercial goal. Nylon will come out of it, and an industry
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1928, DuPont hires a thirty-one-year-old chemist, Wallace Carothers, to run a fundamental research laboratory. The brief is unusual for a company: work with no commercial objective.

Carothers chooses a question that was then contested. Do giant molecules exist?

## The quarrel over macromolecules

The chemistry of the day is divided. For one school, what we call rubber, cellulose, or silk is merely an aggregate of small molecules, held together by poorly identified forces. For the other, a minority, they are true molecules, made of thousands of atoms bound by ordinary chemical bonds.

The debate is not only theoretical. It determines whether one can hope to *manufacture* such materials, or only extract them from what nature produces.

Carothers settles it by manufacture. If macromolecules exist, it should be possible to build them at will, by chaining simple units to one another.

His team succeeds. It produces chains of increasing mass, characterizes them, and shows that their properties, viscosity and mechanical strength, track length steadily. The question of principle is settled: a molecule can be immense, and we know how to make one.

## The thread drawn from a beaker

In 1935, the team obtains a polyamide by reacting two molecules with six carbons each. The product, designated by the code 6-6, melts at a high temperature and can be drawn cold into a filament.

That drawing is the decisive gesture: it aligns the chains with one another, and what was only a paste becomes a remarkably strong fiber.

DuPont sees it as a synthetic silk. Nylon is presented to the public in 1938 and goes on sale in 1940 in the form of stockings. The first stocks sell out within hours. Then the war requisitions production for parachutes, ropes, and tires.

## What the story doesn't tell

Carothers saw none of this. Subject for years to severe depressive episodes, he took his own life in April 1937, at forty-one. He witnessed neither the launch nor the success of what his laboratory had produced.

That laboratory, for its part, established a practice. DuPont had funded research with no intended application, on a disputed theoretical question; an entire industry came out of it, along with the model of the fundamental research laboratory within a company.

The usual order of the story, a need, then research, then a product, is turned upside down here. Nobody was looking for a fiber. The aim was to find out whether a molecule could be large, and the answer incidentally produced the material that part of the world is made of.

carte.punch: Nobody was looking for a fiber. The aim was to find out whether a molecule could be large.
carte.idee: In 1928, DuPont funds a laboratory with no commercial objective. There, Carothers establishes the existence of macromolecules by making them, and incidentally gets nylon out of it. He died before the launch.

quiz.question: What was Carothers looking for when his team obtained nylon?
choix: A cheap substitute for silk, whose import was costly
A fiber strong enough to equip the army with ropes and parachutes
To establish whether very large molecules could really exist
A material capable of replacing natural rubber in tires
quiz.explication: The laboratory had an explicit mandate to work with no commercial objective, on a theoretical controversy: do macromolecules exist? The fiber was a by-product of the demonstration. Military uses and the replacement of silk came afterward, once the material had been obtained.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was the scientific debate over the existence of macromolecules divided in the 1920s?
choix: One school saw mere aggregates of small molecules, the other true giant molecules
All chemists already agreed on the existence of molecules of several thousand atoms
The debate pitted only American chemists against European chemists
The controversy concerned only the chemical definition of the word fiber
quiz_supplementaire.explication: For a majority school, rubber or silk were merely aggregates of small molecules; for the other, a minority, they were true giant molecules bound by ordinary chemical bonds.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What precise technical gesture turns the polyamide paste obtained by Carothers's team into a strong fiber in 1935?
choix: Prolonged heating of the polyamide at very high temperature for several days
Adding a chemical solvent that hardens the material before it cools
Cold drawing, which aligns the molecular chains with one another
Compressing the polyamide under very high pressure in a metal mold
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text presents cold drawing as the decisive gesture: it aligns the chains with one another, and what was only a paste becomes a remarkably strong fiber.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened to Wallace Carothers before nylon's public launch in 1938?
choix: He resigned from DuPont to found his own independent research laboratory
He took his own life in April 1937, without witnessing the launch or the success of nylon
He was fired by DuPont following a disagreement over commercial strategy
He left chemistry to devote himself entirely to university teaching
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Subject for years to severe depressive episodes, Carothers took his own life in April 1937, at forty-one, without having witnessed either the launch or the success of his discovery.
